title: Words ending in -al, es, and no
timingSource: Local Whisper transcription of the official LT download, word-level anchors. Spot-check pending.

cards.title: Why English gives you a head start
cards.body: English is a Germanic language, but a large part of its vocabulary came from Latin. Spanish grew out of everyday spoken Latin, so many of those Latin-origin English words have close Spanish relatives. A few simple patterns let you convert a lot of them; the lesson estimates around 3,000.
cards.caveat: This works for Latin-origin words, not for everyday Germanic words like 'house' or 'dog'.

cards.title: Pattern: English -al → Spanish -al
cards.body: Many English words ending in -al are spelled the same, or almost the same, in Spanish. What changes is the sound: in Spanish the stress moves to the end of the word, onto the -al.
cards.caveat: It's a strong tendency, not a guarantee — and the spelling can change slightly (you'll see illegal → ilegal, annual → anual).

cards.title: Pronounce the vowels as they're written
cards.body: English vowels shift sound a lot (the 'a' in apple vs. mare). Spanish vowels don't: a, e, i, o, u always keep one clear sound each. Read the spelling, give each vowel its pure sound, and your accent improves straight away.

cards.title: es = is (and more)
cards.body: Es means 'is'. The same word covers it is, he is, she is, and 'you are' when you're speaking to someone formally. Put it in front of an -al word and you already have a sentence.

examples.en: It is normal. / He is normal.

cards.title: Watch the S in es
cards.body: English often pronounces a written s as 'z' (think of 'is'). In Spanish, keep it a crisp 's': es sounds like 'ess', never 'ez'.

cards.title: legal / ilegal
cards.body: Two more -al words. In ilegal, notice the spelling: Spanish has one l, not two. The i sounds like the i in 'ink' and the e like the e in 'elephant' — two different sounds, unlike English where both come out similar.

cards.title: You don't need 'he' or 'she'
cards.body: When it's clear who you mean, Spanish simply leaves out the word for he, she or it. Es liberal can mean 'he is liberal' — the context tells you who.

cards.title: Spanish is phonetic
cards.body: Each letter stands for a consistent sound, so you can usually pronounce a new word just from its spelling. The trap is to say the English word with a 'Spanish-sounding' accent; instead, read the letters and say them as written.

cards.title: no = not
cards.body: To make a sentence negative, put no in front of the verb. The word is the same as English 'no', just with a Spanish 'o'. No es = it isn't, he/she isn't, you (formal) aren't.
cards.caveat: Order matters: no goes before es, never after it.

cards.title: ideal — every vowel counts
cards.body: Go letter by letter: i (like ink), e (like elephant), a (like apple). Three separate vowel sounds, stress at the end.

cards.title: More -al words
cards.body: The pattern keeps working. Same spelling, Spanish vowels, stress on the end.

cards.title: anual — drop the extra sounds
cards.body: English 'annual' slips in a 'y' sound (an-yoo-al) that isn't in the spelling. Spanish follows the letters, so there's no 'y'. Spanish also writes it with one n.

cards.title: Link new words to ones you know
cards.body: Tooth is diente. Instead of memorising it as a random word, connect it to English 'dental' (Spanish dental). Spotting the family resemblance makes new vocabulary much easier to remember.

cards.title: A few more
cards.body: More words that follow the same -al pattern.
cards.pron: Spanish v sounds very close to a soft b — a general pronunciation note, not covered in this lesson.

cards.title: No rule? Make a smart guess
cards.body: Not every word has a conversion rule. If you know verbal → verbal, you can guess that 'verb' is close too — often you just add an -o, -e or -a. It's verbo. Guessing vocabulary is fine: if you're wrong, someone will correct you and you'll learn it.

cards.title: Guess words, think through structure
cards.body: Two different attitudes: with vocabulary, guess freely. With sentence building, slow down and think each step through rather than guessing.
cards.caveat: This lesson ends here; the next lesson continues building on es and no.

practice.why: es = it is, and normal stays normal.
no goes in front of es: no es = it isn't.
Leave out 'he' — es alone covers it when context is clear.
Spanish ilegal has a single l.
no + es, then ideal (spelled like English).
No word for 'she' needed: es natural.
Spanish anual has one n, and no 'y' sound.
es also means 'you are' when speaking formally.
From verbal → verbal, guess verb and add -o: verbo.
